references.text: The direct parallel to Gen 10:7, which lists the same sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca, and the sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.
The kings of Sheba and Seba are mentioned as those who bring gifts, reflecting the names Seba and Sheba from Cush's lineage.
Cush and Seba are mentioned together, reflecting the father-son relationship described in Gen 10:7.
Dedan (v. 20) and Sheba (v. 22) are mentioned among the merchants trading with Tyre, pointing to the descendants of Raamah and their role in trade.
Sheba and Dedan are mentioned together with the merchants from Tarshish in connection with Gog's invasion, indicating their continued presence as traders.
Sheba and Dedan are also mentioned as descendants of Abraham through Keturah, showing that the same names appear in multiple lineages.
Cush as a son of Ham provides the necessary overarching context for his own sons.
Complex connection: The same names (Saba/Sheba and Dedan) are linked to different fathers (Raamah/Cush vs. Jokshan/Abraham), challenging the reader to understand the structure of the genealogies.
Cush's uncle Shem and his sons provide the overarching context for Noah's three sons and the distribution of the nations.
The sons of Aram (Shem's branch) provide the broader context for Noah's three sons and their respective genealogies, parallel to Cush's branch.
The conclusion of the entire genealogy (Genesis 10:32) provides the theological context for why Cush's sons are listed: to show the spread of the nations.
